title: US Outposts Were Dangerous Bubbles: How the War on Terror Trapped Itself
dek: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became magnets for conflict. The harder they fought, the heavier they got, losing mobility until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.
why: Wesley Morgan served in Afghanistan and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the War on Terror: tactical success coexisting with strategic failure. Worth pondering for anyone who cares about war and organizations.
who: Readers interested in war history, US military tactics and organizational behavior, especially those curious about the inside story of the War on Terror and how military decisions get made.

points.h: The outpost became a dangerous bubble
points.body: In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan went into Afghanistan's Pech Valley with the troops and found that US outposts meant to provide security for villages had in fact become ‘dangerous bubbles’ that drew conflict toward the villagers. Both the Americans and the enemy suffered few casualties; it was the villages outside the outposts that truly suffered. That contrast made him start asking: who built these outposts, why, and when — questions that ultimately became his book The Hardest Place.

points.h: The US military grew heavier and dumber
points.body: From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tethered to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006 the 10th Mountain Division could still reach remote areas by pickup and ATV, but by 2010, because of the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could barely get to those places and had to rely on special forces for offensive missions. This overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the earlier reach.

points.h: Two ODA teams: restraint versus recklessness
points.body: In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an ‘ink spot’ approach, trying to build secure zones around district centers, and refused to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to get into the Korengal looking for a fight, and ended up entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, used as muscle by one faction, starting the Korengal ‘snowball’ that eventually became a fierce battlefield lasting years.

points.h: Three US tribes inside the military were incompatible
points.body: In eastern Afghanistan there were three ‘tribes’ within the US military: conventional forces; the Green Berets (working with local partners such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police); and the joint special operations task force (such as Task Force 373, made up mainly of SEAL Team Six and Rangers, conducting night raids). The three had different objectives and sometimes supported each other, but more often got in each other's way. For example, the task force might kill someone conventional forces could easily have arrested, while in remote areas conventional forces could not reach, only the task force could operate. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghanistan war.

points.h: Commanders measured success with the wrong metrics
points.body: Many commanders lacked real understanding of counterinsurgency and could only rely on quantifiable performance metrics: ordnance dropped, miles of road built, number of meetings held. The book gives an example: 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, fought in Kunar Province for 15 months and lost 24 soldiers; its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent and 10,000 Beanie Babies handed out — metrics that could not reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force generals and admirals have a chapter in their résumés utterly unlike the standard career path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces — submarine officers, nuclear engineers, naval aviators. For example, current INDOPACOM commander Sam Paparo led the Nuristan PRT for a year. These assignments coincided with the fighting at Wana and Narisan, and they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. That experience became a unique mark on their careers.

points.h: Military-media relations went from transparent to hostile
points.body: Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which unit to embed with, and public affairs just helped him reach company- and platoon-level units. But today, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, military-media relations have deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of officers at battalion level and below sees the media as something terrifying. He argues the turning point was not the McChrystal affair but after Obama's second term, when the military began restricting embeds and pushing the war out of sight, because the complicated message that ‘advisors’ were really ‘combat advisors’ was unwelcome.

points.h: How Multicam became a badge of the elite
points.body: Morgan tells the story of how Multicam spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art-school graduate, lost the Army's camouflage competition (the Army chose the poorly performing ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted Multicam privately because ACU performed badly at night. It then spread through special forces and became a badge of the elite. Crucially, Crye hinted to game producers that this was elite camouflage, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photos did, building an elite image in the minds of young soldiers.
